title: Has the leaning tower of presumed health benefits from ‘moderate’ alcohol use finally collapsed?

claims.statement: In adults followed in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death (published 1981 to 2021, mostly from North America, Europe and Australia), drinking a little (about 1.3 to 25 g of ethanol a day, from one 10-g drink a week to about two drinks a day) compared with not drinking: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of dying from any cause, and the question is disputed. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them, who in most studies included people who had stopped drinking or drank occasionally, people who drank a little died at lower rates: in a 2006 pooled analysis of 34 cohorts (1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths) the death rate was lowest at 6 g a day, about half a drink (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), and stayed lower up to 42 g a day; in 87 and then 107 cohorts (up to 4,838,825 people and 425,564 deaths) the relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90, and 0.83 to 0.88). These analyses give relative risks only, so the difference cannot be given as a number out of 100 (editors' observation). The difference shrinks or disappears as the comparison group is defined more strictly: people who had stopped drinking, some of them because of illness, died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38); against occasional drinkers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment), while abstainers had a higher one with limited adjustment (1.19, 1.12 to 1.27) but not after adjustment (1.04, 0.94 to 1.16); after adjustment for study characteristics, including how each study defined its non-drinkers, the estimate was 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107; in the 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk it was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06); and in the 6 cohorts that did so and had recruited people at a median age of 55 or younger, 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers. Even in 2006, cohorts whose comparison group left out former and light drinkers showed a smaller reduction (16% against 23% at the lowest point) that ended at 30 rather than 52 g a day. The 2016, 2023 and 2024 analyses are by one research group and reuse the same cohorts; the 6-cohort estimate rests on studies the article does not name and allows anything from a 13% lower to an 11% higher death rate (editors' arithmetic); and genetic studies, which avoid the non-drinker comparison, concern heart disease and diabetes rather than deaths from all causes (see the answers on the heart). None of these designs can show whether drinking a little itself makes people live longer or shorter. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Di Castelnuovo et al. 2006 (34 cohorts, 56 curves, 1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths; fixed-effect; against each study's lowest-intake category): lowest relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83) at 6 g a day, lower mortality significant up to 42 g a day; adjusted at least for age 17% lower (99% CI 15% to 18%) at 6 g, up to 37 g; with light or former drinkers in the reference group 23% (20% to 26%) at 8 g, up to 52 g; without them 16% (14% to 18%) at 5 g, up to 30 g; the same 34 curves 19% (17% to 21%) crude and 16% (14% to 18%) adjusted. Stockwell et al. 2016 (87 cohorts, 3,998,626 people, 367,103 deaths), low volume 1.30 to 24.9 g a day: against study-defined abstainers 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90), occasional 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), former 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31); against occasional drinkers, low volume 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10), abstainers 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27); with all study-level covariates, low volume 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07), former 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54); six covariates 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94); 13 lifetime-abstainer studies 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), former 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57); 7 higher-quality studies 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) without one influential study. Zhao et al. 2023 (107 cohorts, 4,838,825 people, 425,564 deaths): unadjusted low volume 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88); fully adjusted 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01; P = .07), occasional 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06), former 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42); against occasional drinkers, fully adjusted, low volume 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11), abstainers 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); I2 above 85.87% in every category. Stockwell et al. 2024 (subgroups of the 107; random study effect): all 107, 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88; 99 studies with low-volume estimates); 6 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger against lifetime abstainers 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without the random effect; with a 30-day intake measure as well, 5 studies, 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15); older cohorts with both abstainer biases, 18 studies, 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89); one criterion only, 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92; 51 studies) and 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95; 18 studies); editors' calculation of the difference between 0.98 and 0.84, treating the two sets of studies as independent: ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), p of about .03. No absolute death rates by drinking group in any of the four.
